query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys reported to date commonly contain both solid solutions and intermetallic compounds. Induction-melted Al- and Mg-rich alloys reached densities of 2.64–2.75 g/cm3 but all had complex structures; Al20Be20Fe10Si15Ti35 combined a density of 3.91 g/cm3 with 911 HV hardness and oxidation resistance at 700 and 900 °C; compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd showed region-dependent compression, plasticity, and corrosion behavior; and reported AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys contained a primary BCC constituent together with intermetallic compounds, with x = 1.0 showing the best property combination in that series. Prior studies have emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, whereas interfacial segregation, interfacial energy, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance remain insufficiently studied. The design must retain a density below 6 g/cm3 and address performance constraints associated with the tendency of Mg and dissimilar constituent elements to form stable intermetallic compounds. Starting from an as-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a metastable solid-solution-plus-intermetallic state, what single intervention hypothesis could improve its combined mechanical, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation performance? State the intervention, its proposed causal mechanism, quantitative or directional predictions relative to the as-processed baseline, the composition and operating or test boundaries, the prior experimental evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a controlled experiment with explicit observations that would falsify it.

generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a Ti-rich surface film
generation.mechanism: Derived from materials-science principles, as the formation of a Ti-rich surface film can improve corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved combined mechanical, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation performance

falsification_experiment.design: High-temperature oxidation and corrosion testing of Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys with and without Ti and Zn additions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Ti and Zn does not improve the combined mechanical, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation performance, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This study investigated the effects of composition and processing on the microstructure, hardness, elastic modulus, and corrosion resistance of spark plasma sintered Mg-Ti-Zn alloys. Key findings include: MgTiZn and Mg4TiZn alloys were produced via ball milling and spark plasma sintering. XRD, SEM, and STEM analyses revealed the presence of multiple phases. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high hardness and stiffness, which were much higher than those of any commercial Mg alloy. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high corrosion resistance (indicated by the high corrosion potential and low corrosion current density) and passivation, which were attributed to the formation of a Ti rich surface film. These findings demonstrate the potential of combining mechanical alloying and SPS to engineer Mg-containing multi-principal element alloys with a rare combination of high hardness and corrosion resistance. This strategy offers a new pathway for designing lightweight structural or biomedical materials that overcome the traditional strength–corrosion trade-off in Mg and Zn alloys. Lightweight complex concentrated alloys (LWCCA), composed of elements with low density, have become a great area of interest due to the high demand in a large number of applications. Previous research on LWCCAs was focused on high entropy multicomponent alloy systems that provide low density and high capability of solid solution formation. Present research introduces two alloy systems (Al-Cu-Si-Zn-Mg and Al-Mn-Zn-Mg-Si) that contain readily available and inexpensive starting materials and have potential for solid solution formation structures. For the selection of appropriate compositions, authors applied semi-empirical criteria and optimization software. Specialized modeling software (MatCalc) was used to determine probable alloy structures by CALPHAD, non-equilibrium solidification and kinetic simulations. The selected alloys were prepared in an induction furnace. Specimens were heat treated to provide stable structures. Physicochemical, microstructural, and mechanical characterization was performed for the selected alloy compositions.
